items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Barnacles are the toughest animals to be found anywhere along a rocky shore at low tide.
choices.B: Tide pool animals are built to survive swings in heat and salt that the open sea never brings.
choices.C: Tide pools are calm, protected places where small sea creatures stay safe from the harsh ocean.
choices.D: Sudden rainstorms are the most serious threat facing ocean animals nearly everywhere in the world.

items.explanation: The passage lists the pools' fast swings in temperature and salt, shows the animals' equipment for meeting them, and ends by calling them “specialists in a kind of hardship.” The choice calling the pools calm and protected is exactly the comfortable idea the third paragraph exists to correct, and the choice about barnacles offers one animal as the whole point. Strategy: choose the choice that covers the whole passage, not one example.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: According to the passage, how do sea stars avoid the worst of the sun?

choices.A: They swim out into deeper water and wait there until the tide returns.
choices.B: They travel back to a shallow groove worn into the rock.
choices.C: They pull a set of hard plates shut over their soft bodies.
choices.D: They slide under ledges and into cracks the light cannot reach.

items.explanation: The second paragraph states that when the sun is high, sea stars slide under ledges and into cracks the light cannot reach. Pulling hard plates shut belongs to the barnacle, and travelling back to a worn groove belongs to the limpet. Strategy: check that the detail belongs to the animal the question names.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The passage suggests that a limpet travels back to its own groove before the water leaves because

choices.A: other limpets are unable to reach that part of the rock at all.
choices.B: the rock inside the groove stays cooler than any other place on the shore.
choices.C: its shell seals tightly against the worn stone and keeps water in.
choices.D: the groove holds bits of food that the limpet has stored there for later.

items.explanation: The paragraph is about equipment for staying wet — the barnacle traps a reserve of seawater — and it says the limpet's shell fits the worn stone tightly, which is what the return trip buys. The choice about cooler rock borrows the sea star's shade, which the passage never connects to the groove. Strategy: combine two nearby facts rather than making a leap.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: In the second paragraph, *reserve* most nearly means

choices.A: a store kept back for later use.
choices.B: a quiet, shy way of behaving around others.
choices.C: an order for a seat placed ahead of time.
choices.D: a wild area set aside to protect animals.

items.explanation: The barnacle traps seawater “enough to keep its body damp until the ocean comes back,” so the reserve is a store saved for later. The protected-area meaning is a real sense of the word and the one a nature passage invites, but a barnacle's shell is not a wildlife preserve. Strategy: test each dictionary meaning inside the actual sentence.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The third paragraph mainly serves to

choices.A: correct a comfortable idea about tide pools and say what the pools really demand.
choices.B: offer one more example of the special equipment a shore animal carries.
choices.C: explain how fish from deep water are collected and studied by scientists.
choices.D: describe how the pools look to someone standing at a distance from the shore.

items.explanation: It opens “It would be a mistake to picture a tide pool as a gentler ocean” and ends by calling the pool the harsher place. The choices about another animal's equipment and about the view from a distance describe the two paragraphs before it, not this one. Strategy: ask what a paragraph does to the ones around it, not only what it mentions.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The author's attitude toward the animals of the tide pool is best described as

choices.A: amused by how small and helpless the pool creatures are.
choices.B: worried that the pools along the rocky shore will soon disappear.
choices.C: doubtful that they truly survive the changes described.
choices.D: respectful of how well suited they are to a difficult place.

items.explanation: “Equipment, not luck” and “specialists in a kind of hardship” credit the animals with skill instead of pitying them, which rules out the amused reading. Strategy: judge attitude from the author's word choices about the subject, not from the topic alone.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Home delivery of mail to farmhouses was the most important change of the 1890s.
choices.B: Bicycles could travel over deep, muddy roads more easily than heavy wagons could.
choices.C: Farmers in the 1880s did not care at all what condition their dirt roads were in.
choices.D: A campaign by bicycle riders prepared the roads automobiles would later use.

items.explanation: The passage follows one thread from the riders' Good Roads campaign to the surveys, road departments, and public money that were “already in place” when cars arrived. The choice about mail delivery takes a single step in that chain and inflates it into the whole story. Strategy: a main idea has to account for the final paragraph too.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Post Office require before it would carry letters to a farmhouse?

choices.A: That a local cycling club map and inspect the route first.
choices.B: That the route be one a mail wagon could travel all year.
choices.C: That each farm family pay a small yearly fee for the service.
choices.D: That the road be paved with stone from end to end.

items.explanation: The third paragraph says the Post Office “would only serve routes a mail wagon could travel all year.” The choice about a cycling club mapping the route takes a real detail about the clubs, which mapped the worst stretches, and attaches it to the wrong group. Strategy: match the requirement to the group that actually set it.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Why did counties that had refused to spend a dollar begin to build roads?

choices.A: A bad road had begun to cost farm families something they wanted.
choices.B: Automobiles had already worn the county's dirt roads down past repair.
choices.C: Farmers had stopped using the heavy wagons that cut ruts in the roads.
choices.D: The cycling clubs had offered to pay for all of the work themselves.

items.explanation: Once a good road was “the difference between getting the mail and not getting it,” paving stopped being a favor to visiting riders and became a local need. The choice about automobiles reverses the passage's order, since cars became common only after these changes. Strategy: look at the sentence just before a result to find its cause.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: In the second paragraph, *mounted* most nearly means

choices.A: grew steadily larger in size.
choices.B: fastened onto a board or a wall.
choices.C: organized and carried out.
choices.D: climbed up onto something tall.

items.explanation: The clubs “mounted a campaign they called Good Roads,” and the next sentence lists the doing of it: printing pamphlets, mapping stretches, asking legislatures for money. Climbing up onto something is the meaning a reader expects in a passage full of bicycles, but no one climbs onto a campaign. Strategy: let the sentence after the word show which meaning is at work.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The sentence “The argument changed when the mail changed” mainly serves to

choices.A: list all of the printed pamphlets and route maps that the cycling clubs produced.
choices.B: repeat the farmers' objection about taxes and city sportsmen in different words.
choices.C: explain the way the mail had been carried to farm families in earlier centuries.
choices.D: mark the point after which paving was no longer dismissed as a favor to city riders.

items.explanation: It stands between the farmers' complaint about city sportsmen and the counties that suddenly began to build, so it announces a switch in reasons. The choice about repeating the objection misses that the sentence overturns the complaint rather than restating it. Strategy: a short sentence set between longer passages usually marks a turn.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: In the last sentence, saying that drivers “owed a debt to people who had been pedaling” means that

choices.A: the author wishes that automobiles had never replaced bicycles at all.
choices.B: drivers benefited from work that cyclists had done for reasons of their own.
choices.C: drivers should have repaid the old cycling clubs with money of their own.
choices.D: cyclists handled the early automobiles better than other people did.

items.explanation: No payment appears anywhere in the passage; the debt is figurative, naming a benefit drivers received from a campaign fought for bicycles. The choice about repaying the clubs with money takes the figure of speech literally, which is the usual trap in this kind of item. Strategy: ask what an image stands for before accepting its literal sense.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: What does the scene mainly show about Theo?

choices.A: He realizes that his grandmother left him more work than he could manage.
choices.B: He discovers that he is not suited to selling fruit at a busy market stall.
choices.C: He gives up a rehearsed sales line and lets customers judge the fruit themselves.
choices.D: He learns that neat handwriting matters far more than he had ever thought.

items.explanation: Theo breaks off his practiced sentence, hands over a cherry instead of a description, and by four o’clock the crate is empty. The choice about neat handwriting reverses the ending, in which the hastily written, messier line is the one that works. Strategy: let the final sentence test your choice.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: What does Theo do to his price card after the woman buys the cherries?

choices.A: He crosses out a line and adds new words in messier handwriting.
choices.B: He copies the prices onto it from his grandmother’s own list.
choices.C: He throws the card away and writes out a new one from scratch.
choices.D: He props it up against the crate of plums at the end of the table.

items.explanation: The last paragraph says he crossed out one line and wrote underneath “in handwriting that was not nearly as neat.” The choice about propping the card against the plums moves a real detail — the card propped against the scale — to the wrong moment in the scene. Strategy: watch where in the scene each detail happens.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The bowl under the table was most likely put there so that

choices.A: Theo could keep count of how many cherries he had sold.
choices.B: Theo’s grandmother would have something to eat later on.
choices.C: bruised cherries could be kept out of the customers’ sight.
choices.D: customers could taste a cherry before buying.

items.explanation: Theo assumes the bowl is her lunch, but it does its work the instant he offers a cherry to the woman, and he then sets it on the table “where people could reach it.” The lunch choice is what the character guesses, not what the scene shows. Strategy: trust what happens in a scene over what a character assumes.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: In the first paragraph, *mind* most nearly means

choices.A: to be bothered by something.
choices.B: to take care of.
choices.C: to hold in his memory.
choices.D: to obey without arguing.

items.explanation: His grandmother leaves and “for two hours the stall was his to mind,” so he is the one looking after it. Being bothered by something is the meaning most readers meet first, as in “I don’t mind,” but a stall cannot be bothered by anybody. Strategy: substitute each choice into the sentence and hear which one survives.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The dash in “They’re excellent for—” marks the point at which

choices.A: Theo abandons the sentence he practiced and changes his approach.
choices.B: Theo’s grandmother comes back to the stall with the change.
choices.C: the woman in the yellow coat interrupts Theo with another question.
choices.D: Theo forgets the prices he had memorized before the market opened.

items.explanation: The narrator says he stopped “because he could hear how it sounded: like a boy repeating something,” and from there he shows the fruit instead of describing it. The choice about an interruption gives the woman credit for a decision Theo makes on his own. Strategy: punctuation that breaks a sentence often marks the turn of a scene.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The last sentence, about the empty crate and the beautifully arranged plums, is best described as

choices.A: wistful and sad about the end of a long day at the market.
choices.B: quietly amused, setting what looked good beside what actually sold.
choices.C: excited and boastful about how much money Theo managed to earn.
choices.D: sharply critical of the mistakes Theo made over the course of the day.

items.explanation: The plums are called “arranged so beautifully” at the exact moment we learn they did not sell, a small joke the narrator makes without scolding Theo. Reading the line as sharp criticism mistakes gentle humor for blame. Strategy: notice when a detail from the opening returns with its meaning changed.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: A damper is the only device that keeps a very tall tower standing up.
choices.B: Strong wind is the greatest danger that any tall building will ever face.
choices.C: A building that moves at all in the wind has been built incorrectly.
choices.D: A tall building is built to sway a little and then stop quickly.

items.explanation: The passage first explains why a frame is given room to bend and then why engineers work to make the motion fade fast, ending with what they actually measure. The choice naming the damper treats one device as the entire design and ignores the frame's give. Strategy: a main idea must hold both halves of a two-part explanation.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: According to the passage, where is a damper placed in a tower?

choices.A: Inside the outer wall on every floor from top to bottom.
choices.B: Beside the scale model inside the engineers' wind tunnel.
choices.C: High in the building, on cables or on a slick steel surface.
choices.D: Below the ground floor, deep inside the building's foundation.

items.explanation: The third paragraph describes an enormous weight “hung high in the building on cables or resting on a slick steel surface.” The wind tunnel choice reuses the final paragraph, where models, not dampers, are placed. Strategy: reread the sentence that names the thing the question asks about.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The passage suggests that a damper is added mainly to

choices.A: make a building that is already safe feel steadier to the people inside.
choices.B: keep the building from moving at all, even during the hardest storm.
choices.C: make the steel frame far stiffer than it would otherwise have been.
choices.D: lower the cost of putting up a tall tower in a crowded city.

items.explanation: The paragraph says long swaying “feels alarming to the people inside it, even when it is perfectly safe,” and the damper is introduced as the answer to that problem. The choice about stopping all motion ignores “the sway fades in seconds instead of minutes,” which shortens the movement rather than ending it. Strategy: notice the exact problem a device is introduced to solve.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: In the second paragraph, *give* most nearly means

choices.A: a willingness to share things with others.
choices.B: a sudden collapse under a heavy weight.
choices.C: a present that is offered without charge.
choices.D: the ability to bend and spring back.

items.explanation: The frame built with “a measured amount of give” bends, sheds the energy of the gust, and “returns to where it started.” The sudden-collapse choice is tempting because a beam can “give way,” but this frame comes back rather than failing. Strategy: read one sentence past the word before choosing.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The sentence “The harder problem is not the leaning but the lingering” mainly serves to

choices.A: give an example of a tall tower that was damaged in a winter storm.
choices.B: shift the discussion from why buildings bend to how the motion stops.
choices.C: introduce an objection that the author goes on to reject in detail.
choices.D: restate the point of the opening paragraph in stronger, plainer language.

items.explanation: Everything before it explains bending; everything after it explains the damper that shortens the sway. Calling it an objection fails, because the author agrees with the sentence and builds on it instead of answering it. Strategy: read the sentences on both sides to see what a hinge sentence separates.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The last three sentences (“In a wind tunnel … how quickly it stops.”) create a tone of

choices.A: doubt about whether wind tunnel tests are worth the trouble.
choices.B: quiet confidence about what the engineers already know.
choices.C: alarm at how far a tall building moves during a storm.
choices.D: impatience with engineers who measure too many things.

items.explanation: The short, flat sentences — “They already know it will” — present the movement as settled fact rather than a surprise or a worry. Alarm is the reaction the whole passage argues against, beginning with “it is not a flaw.” Strategy: read a passage's closing lines for the author's settled position.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The passage is mainly written to

choices.A: prove that repairing a broken object always costs a school less money than replacing it with a new one.
choices.B: describe the objects that the Thursday repair table at Fenwick Middle School brought back in its first term.
choices.C: explain why building projects such as birdhouses and model bridges should be removed from schools entirely.
choices.D: argue that schools should set aside regular time for repair, because repairing teaches careful attention.

items.explanation: The author asks for “one bench, one box of tools, and one period a week for repair” and says the point of the hour “is to teach a habit of looking.” The choice about the Fenwick table names one supporting example, and the choice about saving money is contradicted by the author's own words that the point “is not to save the school money on chairs.” Strategy: choose the choice that covers the whole argument, not one example.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Thursday repair table bring back during its first term?

choices.A: Forty-one items, every one of them either a lamp or an umbrella.
choices.B: Forty-one items, including eleven lamps and fifteen damaged library books.
choices.C: Four items, one for each of the four students who stayed until June.
choices.D: Fifteen backpacks and nine library books with badly broken spines.

items.explanation: The passage lists forty-one items: eleven lamps, nine backpacks, six umbrellas, and fifteen library books with broken spines. The choice naming four items confuses the four long-term students with the count of objects, and the backpacks-and-books choice swaps those two numbers. Strategy: put your finger on the exact sentence before choosing.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The author would most likely say that a school's repair period is working well when

choices.A: the school spends far less money on new furniture than it did the year before.
choices.B: every broken object brought to the bench is successfully fixed by a student.
choices.C: students finish their repairs faster than a paid repair shop nearby would.
choices.D: students keep coming back after the first excitement and show newcomers what they know.

items.explanation: The author calls four the number worth watching — the students still at the table in June, “showing newcomers how to seat a screw” — so a lasting habit and passed-on skill are the real measure. The choice about furniture savings is ruled out by “not to save the school money,” and the choice about fixing everything by the admission that “some objects truly cannot be mended.” Strategy: infer from what the author calls important, not from what sounds sensible in general.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: As used in the second paragraph, “sound” most nearly means

choices.A: making a loud noise.
choices.B: sturdy and undamaged.
choices.C: cheap and easy to replace.
choices.D: sleeping very deeply.

items.explanation: The sentence contrasts one loose leg with the rest of the chair, so the word describes the parts that are still whole and strong. Making a noise and sleeping deeply are the word's everyday meanings, and neither fits a chair being examined for damage. Strategy: read the whole sentence with each choice substituted in.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: What does the second paragraph do in the author's argument?

choices.A: It offers the first evidence from a real school that a repair table can actually work.
choices.B: It lists the tools and the supplies that a school repair bench would need to buy.
choices.C: It states the objection the author hears most often, grants part of it, and then answers it.
choices.D: It gives up the claim made in the first paragraph and proposes a completely different plan.

items.explanation: The paragraph names the objection the author hears most often (repairing is slower), concedes “That is true,” and then answers it: “the objection mistakes what the period is for.” The choice about evidence from a real school describes the third paragraph, which is where Fenwick appears. Strategy: ask what job each paragraph does for the argument, not just what it mentions.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: In the last paragraph the author writes that the difficulty of repair “does not weaken the case; it sharpens it.” This shows that the author

choices.A: turns a fact that seems to weaken the argument into a reason for it.
choices.B: admits that the argument has finally been defeated by modern machines.
choices.C: is unsure whether repair is really worth teaching to students after all.
choices.D: is making a joke about how complicated modern machines have become.

items.explanation: The author grants that machines are getting harder to open and that some things cannot be mended, then argues that scarcity makes the skill of judging what can be fixed more valuable, not less. The choices about defeat and uncertainty misread a confident closing as a retreat. Strategy: watch what an author does with a fact that seems unhelpful — a strong writer often puts it to work.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The passage is mainly about

choices.A: how ice on the Niagara River trapped a boy on the wrong side for eight long days.
choices.B: how a group of engineers decided that a bridge across the Niagara Gorge could not be built.
choices.C: how a boy's kite took the first line across the Niagara Gorge and made a bridge possible.
choices.D: how suspension bridges are built in northern places with long, cold winters.

items.explanation: The passage opens with the need for “one thin thread” to reach the far side and closes with a bridge standing “where a boy's kite string had gone first.” The eight days of ice are one episode inside that story, and the choice about engineers giving up contradicts the ending. Strategy: the main idea should match the first sentence and the last sentence at once.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: According to the passage, why did Homan Walsh cross to the Canadian side before flying his kite?

choices.A: The rocky gorge was much narrower on the Canadian side than elsewhere.
choices.B: The winter ferry did not run from the American rim at any time in January.
choices.C: The wind in the gorge blew from the Canadian side toward the American side.
choices.D: The five-dollar prize could only be claimed by someone standing on the Canadian rim.

items.explanation: The passage states that the steady wind blew from the Canadian side toward the American side, so a kite launched from the American rim “would be carried away from the crossing.” The choices about a narrower gorge, the prize, and the ferry add reasons the passage never gives, and the walls are described as eight hundred feet apart with no narrow place mentioned. Strategy: a “why” question usually has its answer in the sentence right before or after the action.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The passage suggests that Homan's real advantage over the other contestants was that he

choices.A: had built a far stronger kite than anyone else who entered the contest.
choices.B: had helped the engineers build several other bridges before this one.
choices.C: was the only person the engineer in charge allowed to enter the contest.
choices.D: worked out how the wind moved through the gorge and changed where he started.

items.explanation: The passage says he “understood something the adults seem to have overlooked” and then explains the wind, which is why he ferried across before launching. The stronger-kite choice is unsupported — his kite had to be mended, not upgraded — and a contest open to “whoever” could do it rules out the choice about being the only entrant. Strategy: an inference must be built from details the passage actually supplies.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: As used in the third paragraph (“This time the string held”), “held” most nearly means

choices.A: stayed whole under the strain.
choices.B: carried or grasped in the hands.
choices.C: took place, as a meeting does.
choices.D: contained a certain amount inside.

items.explanation: This flight is set against the earlier one, in which “the line snapped,” so the string this time stayed unbroken while the kite pulled on it. Carrying something in the hands is the first meaning most readers reach for, but nobody is holding the string in that sentence. Strategy: when a familiar word turns up in an odd place, find the sentence it answers and let that decide the meaning.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The last paragraph mainly serves to

choices.A: list the goods that the ferries carried back and forth across the Niagara River.
choices.B: argue that public contests are the best way to solve difficult engineering problems.
choices.C: describe in detail how Homan found his kite on the far bank and then repaired it.
choices.D: show how a string too weak to hold real weight became a cable strong enough for a bridge.

items.explanation: The paragraph moves from string to cord to rope to cable, showing how the smallest beginning grew into the bridge. Finding and mending the kite belongs to the paragraph before it, and the passage never argues that contests are the best way to solve problems. Strategy: match a paragraph to its job, and check that the job is not already done somewhere else.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The closing words, “until a bridge stood where a boy's kite string had gone first,” show that the author views Homan's flight as

choices.A: a lucky accident that the engineers did not really need.
choices.B: a small act that made a much larger structure possible.
choices.C: an ordinary errand that any child nearby could have run.
choices.D: a reckless stunt that the author quietly disapproves of.

items.explanation: Setting the thin string beside the finished bridge in one sentence is the author's way of honoring a small beginning. The lucky-accident reading fails because the engineers announced the contest precisely to get that first line, and the ordinary-errand reading is contradicted by the wind reasoning and the eight-day wait. Strategy: ask what an author's final image is quietly praising.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The passage is mainly about

choices.A: a grandmother who teaches her granddaughter to swim across a lake.
choices.B: a girl who gets thoroughly soaked during an early morning on a lake.
choices.C: a girl who becomes strong enough to row after an hour of hard practice.
choices.D: a girl who discovers that skill, not raw force, is what moves a boat.

items.explanation: The last lines say plainly that Nadia “was not stronger than she had been an hour before” but “had simply stopped fighting the thing she was trying to move.” The choice about growing strong enough is tempting because it is what usually happens in practice stories, but the passage denies it in so many words. Strategy: when a story ends by correcting an expectation, that correction is the main idea.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: What happens the first time Nadia pulls with all her weight?

choices.A: The boat slides forward without a sound and the ripples spread behind in even rings.
choices.B: The blades slap the surface, spray soaks her knees, and the boat barely moves.
choices.C: The heron on the shore is startled by the noise and flies off quickly.
choices.D: One of the wooden oars snaps in half and drops into the cold water.

items.explanation: The second paragraph states that the boat barely moved, the blades slapped the surface, and the spray soaked her knees. The silent forward glide describes the later, corrected stroke, and the startled heron reverses the bird, which watches her and then lifts away “without hurrying.” Strategy: check that a detail belongs to the part of the story the question asks about.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The grandmother most likely says nothing at first because she

choices.A: is annoyed with her granddaughter and has decided not to speak to her again.
choices.B: does not know how to row a boat and so has nothing useful to offer.
choices.C: has quietly fallen asleep in the stern of the boat while Nadia works.
choices.D: wants Nadia to feel the problem herself before she is told how to fix it.

items.explanation: Her silence is called “her way of teaching,” and she speaks only after Nadia's hard pulling has failed, giving three exact instructions. The choice about not knowing how to row is impossible given how expert that advice turns out to be, and her folded hands and watchful stillness rule out sleep. Strategy: when a story labels a behavior, use that label to explain the character's purpose.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: When the grandmother says, “Let it bite,” she means that the blade should

choices.A: drop all the way to the lake bottom.
choices.B: sting the hands sharply and painfully.
choices.C: take firm hold of the water.
choices.D: cut into something with sharp teeth.

items.explanation: The next paragraph shows exactly what she meant: Nadia lowers the blade and feels “the water take hold of it, a firm and surprising grip.” Cutting with teeth is the everyday meaning of the word and has nothing to do with an oar. Strategy: when a word is used oddly, read on — a story often shows you the meaning a sentence later.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The paragraph that begins with the grandmother's instruction is the turning point of the passage because it

choices.A: replaces Nadia's effort with a method, and the boat's behavior changes at once.
choices.B: returns to the heron on the shore in order to slow the whole story down.
choices.C: explains why the lake lies so calm and still early on a summer morning.
choices.D: introduces a new character who takes over the rowing from Nadia herself.

items.explanation: Before it, the boat barely moves and the handles jump from her grip; right after the instruction, the boat “slid forward without a sound” and the ripples spread in even rings. The choice about a new character is false, since the grandmother never rows. Strategy: to find a turning point, compare what is true just before it with what is true just after.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The phrase “the oars quarreled with the water, arguing over every stroke” suggests that

choices.A: the oars were old and creaked loudly in their worn metal locks.
choices.B: the lake was rough and choppy that morning and full of waves.
choices.C: Nadia was muttering complaints to herself the whole time she rowed.
choices.D: Nadia's strokes and the water were working against each other.

items.explanation: Giving the oars a quarrel is a way of picturing effort that fights the water instead of using it, which is why the boat barely moves. The rough-lake choice is contradicted by the opening description of a lake “perfectly still.” Strategy: ask what the figure of speech is describing in plain terms before choosing.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Road salt is the only substance that is able to clear ice from a winter road surface.
choices.B: Sand is spread on the roads in very cold places because it helps tires grip the icy surface.
choices.C: Winter storms across the country have become far more dangerous over the last thirty years.
choices.D: Salt keeps water from freezing on roads, but within limits and at a cost, so crews now use less.

items.explanation: The passage explains how salt works, states the temperature limit, describes the harm meltwater carries into soil and streams, and ends with brine spraying that “uses far less salt.” The sand choice is one detail from the second paragraph, and the claim that salt is the only ice remover is contradicted by the sand crews use in the coldest places. Strategy: a main idea has to cover the turn as well as the opening.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: According to the passage, why do trucks spread salt before the snow begins to fall?

choices.A: Because salt melts ice much faster while the pavement is still dry and clear.
choices.B: To keep a thin film of water from freezing onto the pavement in the first place.
choices.C: Because the trucks cannot drive safely on a road once the snow has covered it over.
choices.D: Because salt loses all of its melting power once the crystals become wet.

items.explanation: The first paragraph says the salt “is not there only to melt ice that has already formed” but to stop a film of water from freezing onto the pavement to begin with. The choice about salt losing its power when wet is contradicted by the last paragraph, where crews deliberately dissolve salt into brine before spraying it. Strategy: read the sentence that follows a “not only” — it usually carries the real answer.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Based on the passage, in which situation would a crew be most likely to choose sand instead of salt?

choices.A: A week when the crew's main goal is to lower the freezing point of water on the pavement.
choices.B: A wet afternoon in early spring when the temperature stays near fifty degrees.
choices.C: A night when the temperature is expected to fall to twenty below zero.
choices.D: A storm arriving at thirty degrees, when the crew wants to stop ice from forming at all.

items.explanation: Salted water stays liquid only down to about six degrees below zero; colder than that the salt is “simply cold grit,” which is why the coldest places use sand. The choice about lowering the freezing point is ruled out by the flat statement that “sand cannot lower a freezing point at all.” Strategy: apply the limit the passage gives to the numbers in each choice.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: As used in the first paragraph, “solution” most nearly means

choices.A: a liquid with something dissolved in it.
choices.B: a hard crust of salt and ice on the road.
choices.C: an answer to a difficult problem or puzzle.
choices.D: a plan that a city government agrees to follow.

items.explanation: The sentence describes what forms when salt particles dissolve in water and then stay liquid below freezing, so the word names the salty liquid itself. The answer-to-a-problem sense is the word's everyday meaning and is especially tempting because the passage is about solving a winter problem. Strategy: prefer the scientific sense when the sentence is describing what a substance is, not what someone decided.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: What is the purpose of the short sentence “There is a limit.”?

choices.A: It explains why many crews now spray brine on the pavement before a storm.
choices.B: It simply repeats the main point of the first paragraph in fewer words.
choices.C: It marks a turn from how salt works to the conditions in which it stops working.
choices.D: It introduces the harm that meltwater does to roadside trees and to streams.

items.explanation: Everything before it explains why salted water stays liquid; everything after it gives the freezing point, the minus-six limit, and the switch to sand. The meltwater harm and the brine spraying are real parts of the passage, but they come later, in the third and fourth paragraphs. Strategy: a short sentence set on its own is usually a hinge — read what changes right after it.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The closing sentences — “The chemistry has not changed. What has changed is how carefully it is spent.” — suggest that the author sees the switch to brine as

choices.A: a change in everyday practice, not a new scientific discovery.
choices.B: a sign that scientists no longer agree about how water freezes.
choices.C: proof that road salt has stopped working the way it once did.
choices.D: a warning that brine harms the streams more than dry salt does.

items.explanation: The pair of sentences separates the science, which is unchanged, from the habit of using less of it, which is what crews have altered. The choice calling brine more harmful is contradicted by the same paragraph, which says brine “uses far less salt.” Strategy: when an author sets two short sentences against each other, the second one carries the point.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: A bird's color depends on the food that the bird eats.
choices.B: A feather's color disappears once the feather is crushed.
choices.C: Each branch of a feather holds a layer of keratin.
choices.D: A jay's blue comes from structure, not from a pigment.

items.explanation: The passage opens by showing that grinding a jay's feather takes the blue away, explains that the color comes from the spacing of air pockets, and closes by saying the jay makes its blue rather than carrying it. Saying a bird's color comes from its food describes only the cardinal, which the passage brings in to contrast with the jay. Strategy: the main idea has to hold true for the beginning and the ending, not just one example in the middle.

why.A: That is how the cardinal's red is made, and the passage offers it as the opposite case to the jay, not as the rule for both birds.
why.B: The red feather ground to powder leaves red dust, so crushing a feather does not take every color away — only a color that depends on an arrangement can be crushed out of one.
why.C: The passage does say this, which is why it feels familiar, but it is one small piece of the explanation rather than the point the whole passage is making.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: According to the passage, what happens when a red feather is ground into powder?

choices.A: The dust turns a dull brown, as the jay's did.
choices.B: The dust left in the palm is still red.
choices.C: The dust keeps a faint trace of pink.
choices.D: The dust looks red at certain angles.

items.explanation: The third paragraph states that a red feather ground to powder leaves red dust in the palm, because the color is a pigment and a pigment is a thing you can hold. The dull brown dust belongs to the jay's feather in the first paragraph. Strategy: check which bird the detail belongs to before you pick it.

why.A: Dull brown dust is what the jay's feather leaves behind, and the passage brings the red feather in precisely because it behaves differently.
why.C: The passage calls the dust red, with nothing to suggest the color weakens when the feather is ground.
why.D: No angle is mentioned for the dust; the passage's second test is about light coming through from behind, not about where a viewer stands.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: A feather from an unfamiliar bird is ground to powder, and the powder is still orange. The passage best supports concluding that

choices.A: the feather held air pockets arranged inside it.
choices.B: the orange came from a pigment in the feather.
choices.C: the bird eats the same food a cardinal eats.
choices.D: light from behind would turn the feather brown.

items.explanation: The passage sets up a test: a color made by an arrangement disappears when the arrangement is crushed, while a color made by pigment survives, as the red dust does. Orange powder that keeps its color therefore behaves like the cardinal's red and must be a pigment. Strategy: when a question gives you a new case, apply the rule the passage demonstrated rather than looking for the new case in the text.

why.A: Arranged air pockets make a color that lasts only as long as the arrangement does, so a color that survives grinding points away from this answer.
why.C: The passage says a bird builds a pigment from what it eats, but it never says that one pigment means one particular diet.
why.D: Turning brown in light from behind is the jay's result, and this feather has just behaved like the cardinal's, which stays its own color when it is lit that way.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: In the second paragraph, *swallows* most nearly means

choices.A: darts and dives like a small bird.
choices.B: swiftly eats a bite of food.
choices.C: takes it in and absorbs it.
choices.D: sends it straight back to the eye.

items.explanation: The sentence before says the red and yellow light travels deeper into the feather, and it never comes back out, so the dark pigment takes it in. The bird meaning is planted by the subject matter, which is exactly why it is worth testing inside the sentence. Strategy: read the sentence before the word to see what the word is actually doing there.

why.A: A swallow is a bird, and the word is planted in a passage about birds, but here it names what a layer of dark pigment does, and a layer of pigment is not a creature.
why.B: This is the everyday meaning, and a layer of pigment does not eat anything; what reaches it is light.
why.D: Sending light back toward the eye is what the air pockets do with blue, and it is the opposite of what happens to the light that travels deeper in.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The paragraph beginning "A cardinal's red works the other way" mainly serves to

choices.A: set a true pigment beside the jay's kind of blue.
choices.B: give one more example of color made by structure.
choices.C: explain why the cardinal's red is the brighter color.
choices.D: teach a reader how to test a feather at home.

items.explanation: The paragraph begins by saying the cardinal's red works the other way, then describes two tests that come out differently for a pigment and for an arrangement. Its job is comparison, which is why the word other is doing so much work in its first sentence. Strategy: watch the opening sentence of a paragraph for a signal about what the paragraph is for.

why.B: The cardinal's red is a pigment, which is the other kind of color entirely, so this paragraph adds a contrast rather than another example.
why.C: The passage never compares how bright the two colors are; it compares how each one is made.
why.D: Two tests are described, but they are there to show that the two colors behave differently, not to hand a reader a procedure to carry out.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: In the last two sentences, saying that the jay does not carry its blue but makes it suggests that

choices.A: the color happens when light meets the structure.
choices.B: the jay can change its feathers' color at will.
choices.C: the feather works to keep its blue from fading.
choices.D: the feather would be blue even in the dark.

items.explanation: The closing lines draw a line between having a color, the way the cardinal has a pigment you can hold, and making one, which happens only when light strikes the arranged pockets and comes back. Reading makes as effort or as choice turns a figure of speech into a literal claim the passage does not make. Strategy: ask what an author's phrase is contrasted with before deciding what it means.

why.B: The bird is not choosing anything here; makes describes the feather's structure at work, not a decision the jay takes.
why.C: This takes makes to mean effort, and no fading and no effort appear anywhere in the passage.
why.D: The sentence says the blue arrives with the light, and the paragraph before says the blue depends on light bouncing back off a structure.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: A tree's rings record each year's weather, and that record can date old wood.
choices.B: Counting a tree's rings is the surest way to learn how old the tree really is.
choices.C: Trees growing in warm, wet places are of little use to researchers.
choices.D: A wide ring proves that one tree was healthier than the trees near it.

items.explanation: The passage grants that counting rings gives an age, calls that the least interesting thing they can tell you, and then spends two paragraphs on what the widths record and how that record dates a beam from an old roof. The choice about counting for age stops where the first paragraph stops. Strategy: when a passage calls an idea the least interesting thing, the main idea is what comes after it.

why.B: Counting for age is the one use the passage grants and then sets aside as the least interesting thing the rings can tell you, and the last paragraph shows a count can even be off by a year.
why.C: Those trees are one limit named near the end, not what the passage as a whole is about.
why.D: A wide ring is tied to a wet, mild year, not to one tree doing better than its neighbours.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: According to the passage, the ring a reader sees is the line between

choices.A: the pale spring wood and the dark wood of that year.
choices.B: one year's dark wood and next spring's pale wood.
choices.C: the bark of the tree and the new wood beneath it.
choices.D: the wood of a wet year and the wood of a dry year.

items.explanation: The second paragraph names the line outright: the ring you see is where one year's dark wood stops and next spring's pale wood begins. The pale-and-dark pair inside one year is a real boundary but not the one the passage points at, and the new layer of wood goes beneath the bark rather than on it. Strategy: find the sentence that defines the thing and read it exactly.

why.A: Those two do sit side by side within a single year, but the passage points at the other edge — where one year's dark wood stops and the next spring's pale wood begins.
why.C: The tree adds its new layer of wood beneath the bark, so the bark is not the edge being described.
why.D: Wet and dry years give wide and narrow rings, but the line itself is a change from dark wood to pale wood, not a border between two kinds of year.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The passage suggests that the researcher could not date the beam without

choices.A: a mark left on the beam by whoever built the roof.
choices.B: a count of how many rings the beam still holds.
choices.C: rings from trees whose years are already known.
choices.D: a sample taken from the same roof's other beams.

items.explanation: A living tree's outermost ring is this year's, so its rings can be counted back to real years; the beam is dated by sliding its own pattern along that record until the wide and narrow years line up. Without a set of rings whose years are already settled, the beam's pattern is just a pattern with nowhere to sit. Strategy: ask what a method borrows from outside the object it is examining.

why.A: The passage says the beam is dated though nobody wrote a date on it, so a written mark is exactly what is missing.
why.B: Counting tells you how many years the wood grew, not which years those were.
why.D: The pattern is slid along the record kept by living trees, and other beams from the same roof would carry no known years of their own.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: In the third paragraph, *agreement* most nearly means

choices.A: a promise made between two people.
choices.B: the same weather from year to year.
choices.C: a rule about matching word forms.
choices.D: a close match between patterns.

items.explanation: The sentence just before says the bands run in step, so the agreement named next is that matching between trees. The everyday promise-between-people meaning is the trap, and the weather choice lifts a true phrase from the sentence before and attaches the word to the wrong thing — what runs in step is the patterns. Strategy: put your choice into the sentence in place of the word and check that it still describes the same thing.

why.A: That is the word's everyday meaning, but nobody here is promising anything — what is happening is that bands are matching.
why.B: The sentence before does say trees in one region live through the same weather, but that agreement points back at the patterns running in step, and the passage's whole point is that the weather differs from year to year.
why.C: Agreement does mean that in a grammar lesson, where a subject and a verb must match, but this sentence is about bands of wood rather than words.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The last paragraph mainly serves to

choices.A: set out the limits of a method the passage has explained.
choices.B: explain again how a tree lays down wood each spring.
choices.C: argue that ring patterns are too unreliable to use.
choices.D: explain how one beam is matched against the living record.

items.explanation: The paragraph announces that the limits are the ordinary kind and then names them — no clear band where it is warm and wet all year, a skipped year, a doubled one — before closing with the safeguard of checking many trees. Saying ring patterns are too unreliable to use goes further than a paragraph that ends by explaining how researchers work around the trouble, and the matching of a beam to the living record has already happened a paragraph earlier. Strategy: a paragraph that names limits and then a safeguard is qualifying a method, not throwing it out.

why.B: That was settled in the second paragraph; the last one turns to where the method runs into trouble.
why.C: The paragraph raises problems and then closes with the safeguard of checking many trees, which is a caution rather than a rejection.
why.D: Matching a beam against the living record is the third paragraph's job; the last one is about where that matching cannot be trusted.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The comparison in “the rings are a row of entries, one for every year the tree stood” suggests that the rings

choices.A: are written by hand onto the wood.
choices.B: keep a record, one year at a time.
choices.C: are all exactly the same width.
choices.D: grow larger each year of a tree's life.

items.explanation: An entry is a line written in a record, and the passage sets the rings in order with one for every year the tree stood, so the comparison turns the trunk into a year-by-year log. Taking the picture literally, as writing on the wood, misses that a comparison borrows a quality rather than stating a fact. Strategy: with a comparison, ask which quality is being borrowed, not whether the picture is literally true.

why.A: The rings are compared to written entries, but nothing in the passage says anyone writes on the wood.
why.C: The passage says the opposite — wide in a wet, mild year and narrow in a dry, hard one.
why.D: Ring width depends on the weather of that year, not on how old the tree has become.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Sawdust was the coldest material the workers in the ice trade could find.
choices.B: Ice lasted the summer because the walls and the stacking both slowed heat.
choices.C: Ships once carried ice from northern ponds to harbors in far warmer places.
choices.D: Winters in the past were far colder than any winter people now know of.

items.explanation: The passage says the icehouse made no cold of its own and was built only to slow heat down, and then spends two paragraphs on the two ways that was done: doubled walls packed with sawdust, and blocks cut large and stacked tight so little surface was left in the open. The choice about ships is a real detail from the last paragraph, but a detail cannot be the main idea. Strategy: pick the statement the middle paragraphs are busy proving, not the one that appears only once.

why.A: The passage says flatly that sawdust is not cold — its whole usefulness is that heat travels through it badly.
why.C: That is true, but it is one sentence near the end, not what the whole passage is built to explain.
why.D: The passage never compares old winters with modern ones; it only describes what people did with the ice a winter gave them.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: According to the passage, why did workers cut the ice into large blocks instead of small pieces?

choices.A: A large block has less surface than the same ice in pieces.
choices.B: Large blocks were easier for the crews to carry down a hill.
choices.C: Small pieces would have melted before reaching the icehouse.
choices.D: Large blocks sold for a higher price in the warm harbors.

items.explanation: The third paragraph gives the reason directly: ice melts at its surface, and one large block has less surface, for the amount of ice in it, than the same ice chopped into pieces. Less exposed surface means slower melting, which is why workers also stacked the blocks tight and filled the seams. Strategy: when a paragraph states a rule and then a practice, the rule is the answer to "why".

why.B: The passage mentions hauling the blocks but never says the large size made carrying them any easier.
why.C: The passage does say the blocks were hauled some distance, but the reason it gives for cutting them large is about how slowly stored ice melts, not about the trip.
why.D: The passage says nothing about price — only about how quickly ice of different shapes melts.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Based on the passage, which change would most likely make stored ice last longer?

choices.A: Splitting the blocks into smaller pieces before they are stacked.
choices.B: Packing a thicker layer of sawdust between the doubled walls.
choices.C: Leaving wide gaps between the blocks so air can circulate.
choices.D: Rinsing the blocks with cold water before stacking them.

items.explanation: Sawdust is described as a poor path for heat, and the passage concludes that heat which cannot get in cannot melt anything, so a thicker packing in the wall cavity means less heat reaching the ice. The rinsing choice is the tempting one, because cold water sounds helpful; only the passage's own sentence about meltwater — it carries heat into the pile faster than still air could — rules it out. Strategy: apply the reason the passage gives for each practice to see whether a change helps it or fights it.

why.A: Smaller pieces have more surface for the same amount of ice, and surface is exactly what sets the pace of melting.
why.C: Workers did the opposite, stacking the blocks tight and filling the seams so little ice was left in the open.
why.D: Cold water sounds like it should help, but the passage says water lying against the ice carries heat into it faster than still air does.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: In the third paragraph, *standing* most nearly means

choices.A: upright on its feet, not lying down.
choices.B: waiting its turn in a line.
choices.C: lasting on and on for years.
choices.D: not draining away from a place.

items.explanation: The rest of the same sentence explains the word: the floor was sloped, and a floor is sloped for water that would otherwise sit where it lands. Meltwater standing against the pile is meltwater that has not drained away, and that is the water the passage says carries heat into the ice. The upright sense is the one the word usually carries, which is what makes it the trap. Strategy: when a familiar word sits oddly, look for the detail in the same sentence that was built to deal with it — here, the slope.

why.A: That is the word's everyday meaning, but water has no feet; the sentence is about water that stays where it collects.
why.B: Nothing in the passage is queuing — the meltwater is not waiting for anything, it is sitting against the ice.
why.C: "Standing" can mean long-lasting, but this is meltwater running off a pile of ice, and the slope exists to get rid of it quickly.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The sentence "The shape of the stack mattered too" tells the reader that the third paragraph will

choices.A: add another reason the ice melted slowly.
choices.B: repeat the point about sawdust in new words.
choices.C: explain how ships reached the far-off harbors.
choices.D: admit how much of each load melted anyway.

items.explanation: The word "too" adds something to what came before: the second paragraph explained the building, and the third explains the ice, with exposed surface as one more thing that controlled melting. A paragraph that only restated the sawdust point would have no use for "too". Strategy: a small linking word like "too" or "also" usually announces that a new reason is being added to an old one.

why.B: The paragraph leaves the walls behind entirely and talks about the ice itself — its surface, its size, how it was stacked.
why.C: The ships do not appear until the paragraph after this one, and their voyage is not what "the stack" refers to.
why.D: The passage does admit that, but a paragraph later; this sentence is still introducing the ways melting was slowed.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The last sentence, "It was a machine for making winter last," suggests that the icehouse

choices.A: was powered by an engine that the workers ran.
choices.B: made the winter season itself grow longer.
choices.C: held on to winter's ice well into the summer.
choices.D: was more useful in winter than in the summer.

items.explanation: The passage sets the sentence against its opposite — the icehouse was never a machine for making cold — so what it makes is time: ice cut in January is still solid in August. Reading "machine" literally, as something with an engine, misses that the whole sentence is a figure of speech. Strategy: when a sentence says what something is *not* right before saying what it is, use the contrast to pin down the meaning.

why.A: "Machine" is being used as a figure of speech; the building described has walls, a door and a sloped floor, and no moving parts at all.
why.B: No building can stretch a season; what was stretched was the usefulness of one winter's ice.
why.D: The opening says the January work was for July, and the ice was still solid in August — the icehouse earned its keep in the warm months.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: What does the scene mainly show about Ines's job that evening?

choices.A: It taught her to understand the talk as well as Rosa did.
choices.B: It looked like nothing and demanded constant attention.
choices.C: It was harder than she should have been asked to try.
choices.D: It mattered far less to the talk than she had hoped.

items.explanation: The first sentence calls it the easiest job in the hall, and everything after it is work — the failed plan, the red slash, the counting back, the thumb held in place until it wore a crease in the paper. The choice about understanding the talk is ruled out by the passage's own words that the typed words meant almost nothing to her. Strategy: when a story opens by calling something easy, read the rest as the answer to that claim.

why.A: The passage says the typed words "meant almost nothing to her" — she worked from the shapes on the page and the red slashes, not from following what her aunt was saying.
why.C: She finds the job hard and does it anyway; nothing in the passage suggests she was wrongly asked, and by the end she is managing it without looking down.
why.D: The story points the other way: each photograph had to land on the sentence that needed it, and the one that lands correctly is the moment her aunt can keep reading.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: According to the passage, how did Ines know when to change the picture?

choices.A: She listened for the words just before each change.
choices.B: She waited for a nod from her aunt across the room.
choices.C: She counted the sentences as her aunt read them.
choices.D: She watched Rosa's finger reach the red slash.

items.explanation: The fourth paragraph gives the method in order: find the red slash, count back two lines, put a thumb there, get ready when the finger arrives at the thumb, and press when the finger arrives at the slash. Listening for the words is a real detail from the passage, but it is the plan she abandoned. Strategy: check whether a detail describes what the character tried or what actually worked.

why.A: That was her first plan, and the passage says it failed: by the time she heard those words, "they had gone past."
why.B: Rosa never signals her. The passage makes a point of saying Rosa did not glance over, which is why Ines has to find the cue herself.
why.C: The counting in the passage happens once, on paper — two lines back from a slash — and not as a running count through the talk.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: Ines treats her aunt's not glancing over as "the highest compliment available" most likely because it means

choices.A: the picture had not needed changing on that line.
choices.B: the picture came on time and did not interrupt Rosa.
choices.C: Rosa was pleased with how the talk itself was going.
choices.D: Rosa had forgotten that Ines was sitting nearby.

items.explanation: A picture that arrived late or on the wrong sentence would force the speaker to look across and check, so a speaker who never looks across is a speaker who was never interrupted. Reading the line as forgetfulness mistakes being unnoticed for being unneeded, when the whole scene rests on how much Rosa needs her. Strategy: ask what would have happened instead if the character had done the job badly.

why.A: It did need changing, and it changed: the sentence just before says the photograph arrived on the word it belonged to.
why.C: Nothing in the passage reports what Rosa thought of her own talk; the sentence attaches her steadiness to the photograph landing correctly.
why.D: Rosa is depending on her for pictures she cannot change herself, and being forgotten would be no compliment at all.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: In "black clusters where the paragraphs were busy," *busy* most nearly means

choices.A: packed tightly with words.
choices.B: occupied with hard work.
choices.C: noisy and full of movement.
choices.D: hurrying from place to place.

items.explanation: The second half of the same sentence gives the measure: the clusters are black where the paragraphs are busy and white where they thin out, so the word is describing how crowded the printing looks. The ordinary meaning about a person with too much to do is the one to test first and then reject, because a paragraph has no errands. Strategy: when a sentence sets two halves against each other, the second half often defines the first.

why.B: This is the everyday meaning of the word, but it describes a person with a lot to do, and a paragraph on a page has no work to be occupied with.
why.C: A busy street is noisy, but the sentence is about how a printed page looks to someone holding it, not about sound or motion.
why.D: This describes someone rushing about; the paragraphs in the passage are sitting still on a sheet of paper, differing only in how crowded they are.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The three sentences beginning "You sat at a small table" mainly serve to

choices.A: give the reader directions for running the pictures.
choices.B: describe what the rest of the room did during the talk.
choices.C: show the job as Ines pictured it before she tried it.
choices.D: suggest that Ines had been talked into taking the job.

items.explanation: The story steps out of Ines for three sentences to lay out the job the way she expected it, as though it were obvious to anybody — and then drops straight back with the line about her mistake. Everything after that is the same job from the inside: a finger to watch, a slash to find, a thumb to keep in place. Strategy: when a narrator changes who the sentences are about, ask what that change shows which the ordinary telling could not.

why.A: They instruct nobody. They restate what the job sounded like from outside, which is why the very next line calls it a mistake.
why.B: The room is not doing these things; sitting at the small table and pressing the button are Ines's own job, seen before she began it.
why.D: The first sentence says she agreed because of how the job sounded, and the passage never shows anyone persuading her.

items.subject: RC
items.prompt: The comparison "She watched the way a person crossing a street watches" suggests that Ines

choices.A: paid attention to what was coming, not what was here.
choices.B: watched several things happening at the same time.
choices.C: was frightened by the traffic on the road outside.
choices.D: thought the room was as crowded as a busy street.

items.explanation: Someone stepping off a kerb is not watching the empty road in front of them but the car that has not arrived yet, and the rest of the sentence spells the comparison out: ahead of herself, two lines early, her thumb already in place. Taking the street literally turns a figure of speech into a scene the story never has. Strategy: after a comparison, read the words that follow it — the author usually explains the image straight away.

why.B: A busy street is the first thing the word brings to mind, but the rest of the sentence is about being early rather than about watching a crowd.
why.C: There is no traffic in the story; the street is a comparison, not a place anyone goes.
why.D: The comparison is about how she watched, not about how full or noisy the hall was.
